name: When Love Meets Survival
description: Join us for a lecture that asks a different question about the relationships in your life:What if the greatest threat to your relationship is a nervous system that learned long ago that love and danger could exist in the same moment?About the LectureTrauma doesn't knock before entering a conversation. It arrives disguised as defensiveness, withdrawal, perfectionism, people-pleasing, control, jealousy, silence or overwhelming need, shaping what we notice, what we fear, and how we connect.In this experiential lecture, we move beyond "what's wrong with this relationship?" and ask instead: what happened to the people inside it? Through embodied exercises, reflective inquiry and lived experience, we'll explore how trauma lives in the body, organises attachment, and silently choreographs the patterns we call "just how we are" in love.The session explores:The real difference between everyday stress and genuine traumaWhy we're drawn to the partners we choose, beyond attraction and shared interestsHow trauma reshapes the brain and nervous system, and what Polyvagal Theory reveals about safety and threatHow attachment styles and "protective parts" (from Internal Family Systems) shape conflict, intimacy and trustThe relational patterns — pursuer-withdrawer, critic-defender — that keep two nervous systems stuck in the same dancePathways toward emotional safety, repair and genuine connectionAbout the SpeakerProf. Nishtha Kavita Grover is an Assistant Professor, Programme Coordinator and Head of Student Welfare Concerns at the National Forensic Sciences University (NFSU), Delhi Campus. An RCI-registered Child and Adolescent Rehabilitation Psychologist with over eight years of clinical experience, she has worked with paramilitary personnel and trained clinically at NIMHANS. At NFSU, she teaches Clinical Psychology, Forensic Psychology, Criminal Profiling and Trauma Psychology, and is a recipient of the SAP Fellowship for Mental Health. Alongside her academic work, she runs a private psychotherapy practice, working with adolescents, young adults, couples and families on trauma, attachment, anxiety and emotional well-being.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive — unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

name: The Limits of Computation
description: Join us for a lecture that traces one dangerous idea through three brilliant, broken minds:In 1891, Georg Cantor gave us set theory, and then spent years battling for his peace of mind. In 1931, Kurt Gödel proved that any system of logic cannot capture all truths, and later descended into deep paranoia. In 1936, Alan Turing identified problems that no computer can ever solve; and met a tragic end.Three of history's most brilliant minds, circling the same dangerous idea.This lecture plays with diagonalisation — the beautifully unsettling proof technique at the heart of all three discoveries — and explores what it reveals about the limits of logic, mathematics and computation itself. Some ideas don't just describe the edges of what we can know. They seem to press back on the people who find them.The session explores:What diagonalisation is, and why the same idea kept resurfacing across a century of mathematicsHow Cantor's set theory, Gödel's incompleteness theorems and Turing's halting problem are secretly the same argumentWhat it means for a system of logic to be unable to capture all truthsWhy some of history's most brilliant thinkers found this particular idea so disturbingAbout the SpeakerDr. Aalok Thakkar is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Ashoka University. His work focuses on logic in computer science and its applications to programming languages, automata theory, and trustworthy AI.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive — unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

name: Plantation Drive
description: Come join us for a plantation drive in Delhi. Our city is one of the most polluted cities in the world, with nothing bringing relief to its people and other organisms. The drive will focus on native and climate-resilient species carefully chosen for Delhi’s conditions. Saplings will be planted alongside flowering shrubs and understorey plants that support birds, butterflies, and pollinators. These trees have been selected for their ability to filter particulate matter, absorb pollutants, and release oxygen, directly helping combat the city’s air-quality challenges.This planned plantation is to expand green cover, improve air quality, soften the city’s hard edges with shade, and create living spaces where people and wildlife can thrive together. name: In Search Of Djinns : Kotla Feroz Shah Walk
description: The walk takes you inside the fort of the 14th century ruler Firoz Shah Tughlaq built for his new capital Firozabad. The Kushak-e- Firoz (the Palace of Firoz) was strategically built at the banks of River Yamuna. The fort faced riverfront and lush green plains, its staircase leading you to the banks. It has a functioning mosque, a circular baoli (stepwell) known to have water snakes and a hypnotic effect on its visitors (it has recently been barricaded). The fort also has the magnificent Ashokan Pillar in Pali text erected at a height. It is confounding to any visitor how almost 27 tonne of heavy weighing monolith pillar was taken from Haryana and planted inside the fort at such a great height!Every Thursday evening Djinn (supernatural creatures in Islamic mythology) worship is performed in the complex, with visitors leaving their wish list, and a thread tied to the lattice for the Djinns to fulfill their wishes! The fort in recent years has gained the reputation of being haunted, because of the strong belief of Djinns inhabiting the fort.

name: Tughlaqabad - The Cursed City
description: Join me on a journey through Tughlaqabad Fort, one of Delhi’s most imposing medieval ruins, where history is inseparable from legend.Built in 1321 by Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq, founder of the Tughlaq dynasty, the fort was conceived as a formidable capital and military stronghold. Its battered stone walls, immense bastions, and steep defensive slopes still convey the ambition of its founder.But Tughlaqabad is remembered for more than its architecture. The fort is deeply entwined with the story of Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq, his son Muhammad bin Tughlaq, and the oft-repeated legend of the saint Nizamuddin Auliya, whose supposed curse has become part of the fort’s enduring folklore.As we walk through its ruined palaces, gateways and hidden passages, we will look beyond the legends to understand the men, politics and ambitions that shaped one of the most remarkable chapters in Delhi’s history.

name: From The Cradle to The Grave
description: Unbeknown to many, India has slowly put in place welfare for its people in the informal sector.What does this welfare architecture actually look like? Does it reach the people it's meant for? And does it work?About the Lecture This lecture takes a close look at the quiet, decades-long project of building social protection for the hundreds of millions of Indians who work outside the formal economy, without steady paychecks, contracts or safety nets in the conventional sense. Drawing on 25 years of fieldwork across rural India, we'll examine what welfare looks like when it has to be built for people the system was never originally designed around.The session explores:What India's welfare architecture for the informal sector actually looks likeWhere this system succeeds, and where it failsWhat 25 years of fieldwork across rural India reveal about how welfare policy meets lived realityWhy "cradle to grave" is more than a slogan for the majority of India's workforceAbout the SpeakerReetika Khera teaches economics at IIT Delhi, including a course on economics through film. Over the past 25 years, her research has taken her deep into fieldwork across rural India, focusing on social policy, food security, employment and social protection for India's informal workforce. Among lesser-known economists, she recommends Angus Deaton and Diane Coyle — and among recent fiction, Talashnama by Ismail Darbesh, This Is Not That Dawn by Yashpal, The Theft by Abdulrazak Gurnah, David Lodge's Campus Trilogy, Jerry Pinto's The Education of Yuri, Sharankumar Limbale's Dalit Brahmin, and almost anything by John le Carré.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Rooted in Multan, where my own Nani is from, and reaching into Lahore and Sindh - the homes our grandparents carried with them.  This menu brings back food that's slow, laborious, and increasingly rare: a sourdough flatbread fermented over three days, a lotus-stem starter barely made anymore even in Sindhi households, a moth dal kachori you'll mostly only find on a handful of old Delhi streets.Alongside them sit the dishes that never left,  a rich Lahori chicken karahi, a comforting channay, and phirni made exactly the way it's made every Holi in our family, because some things don't need reviving. name: Haunted Walk: Mehrauli Archaeological Park
description: Join us for a hauntingly beautiful night walk through the Mehrauli Archaeological Park, a place where centuries of Delhi’s history come alive—alongside tales of the unseen. In this special segment, Ruhaani Raatein, we delve into the world of djinns, the mystical beings believed to reside in this ancient land.Guided by a historian and storyteller, we’ll explore how djinns are viewed and worshipped in Islamic traditions, and how folklore continues to shape the spiritual character of Mehrauli even today.Our walk will take you through: The tomb of Jamali Kamali, often called the Gay Taj Mahal for its poetic mystique and timeless love story A haunting 500-year-old baoli (stepwell)The remnants of a British-era swimming pool, hidden in plain sight A peaceful lakeside café, perfect for ending the evening with a quiet reflection or a warm chaiAs night falls and shadows grow, let the stories guide you through one of Delhi’s oldest, most magical spaces—where the past is never truly past.
